claims.text: The particles under study are initially solid Fe-Ni-Cr-Co-Cu high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles.
Premelting and melting in Fe-Ni-Cr-Co-Cu nanoparticles are governed by nanoscale atomic segregation.
Nanoscale atomic segregation produces local compositional heterogeneity.
Local compositional heterogeneity produces a distribution of local melting points.
Segregation changes local surface and interface energies.
Variations in bonding and surface or interface energy cause early-stage atomic rearrangements associated with premelting.
Early-stage heterogeneous atomic rearrangements broaden the overall melting transition.
Fe-Ni-Cr-Co-Cu HEA nanoparticles will have a lower premelting-onset temperature than comparable monometallic or bimetallic nanoparticles.
Fe-Ni-Cr-Co-Cu HEA nanoparticles will have a broader melting transition than comparable monometallic or bimetallic nanoparticles.
Monometallic and bimetallic nanoparticles typically have more uniform compositions, sharper melting transitions, and higher premelting-onset temperatures.
Changing the number of constituent elements can change the likelihood of obtaining a random, single-phase alloy when atomic mobility is limited.
Bimetallic particles of matched size and surface characteristics synthesized under identical conditions provide a controlled reduction in chemical complexity.
In situ synchrotron X-ray diffraction can monitor structural changes during nanoparticle formation or thermal treatment.
Differential scanning calorimetry can be used to determine premelting onset and melting-transition width in the proposed particles.
Size effects and high surface energy dominate phase behavior within the proposed applicability regime.
Rapid heating followed by rapid cooling can crystallize homogeneous five-element alloy nanoparticles without segregation or phase separation.
The hypothesis would be falsified if the HEA and bimetallic controls had statistically indistinguishable premelting-onset temperatures and melting-transition widths.
The hypothesis would be falsified if direct measurements found no nanoscale atomic segregation before melting.
